title: Soupy Sichuan-Style Dan Dan Noodles with Pork & Sesame
dek: Springy wheat noodles, savory pork and preserved mustard greens meet a warm chile-sesame broth whose heat can be adjusted bowl by bowl.
image_alt: Soupy dan dan noodles in a red chile-sesame broth with crumbled pork, scallions, peanuts and sesame seeds
ingredients: 1/3 cup finely chopped sui mi ya cai or other preserved mustard greens
1/3 cup Chinese sesame paste, stirred well
2 tbsp chile oil, plus more for serving
1/4 cup roasted unsalted peanuts, roughly chopped
1/4 cup cilantro leaves and tender stems, roughly chopped

instructions.name: Toast and grind the peppercorns
instructions.text: Set a dry 12-inch skillet over medium-low heat. Add the Sichuan peppercorns and toast for 2 to 3 minutes, shaking often, until fragrant but not dark. Cool briefly, then grind finely in a spice grinder or mortar; reserve 1 teaspoon for the broth and save the remainder for another meal.

instructions.name: Brown the pork
instructions.text: Return the skillet to medium-high heat and add the neutral oil. Add the pork and salt, press it into a thin layer and leave it undisturbed for 2 minutes. Break it into small crumbles and cook for 3 to 4 minutes more, until browned and the thickest pieces reach 160°F.

instructions.name: Build the savory topping
instructions.text: Reduce the heat to medium. Stir the garlic, ginger and doubanjiang into the pork for 45 seconds. Add the preserved mustard greens and cook for 2 minutes, stirring, until the mixture is fragrant and no liquid pools in the skillet. Remove from the heat and cover to keep warm.

instructions.name: Mix the sesame base
instructions.text: In a heat-safe bowl, whisk the sesame paste, soy sauce, black vinegar, sesame oil, brown sugar, 2 tablespoons chile oil and the reserved 1 teaspoon ground Sichuan pepper until smooth. Divide this concentrated sauce evenly among four deep serving bowls.

instructions.name: Heat the broth and cook the noodles
instructions.text: Bring the chicken broth to a bare simmer in a small saucepan. Meanwhile, cook the wheat noodles in a large pot of unsalted boiling water according to the package directions until just tender. Drain immediately and shake off excess water; do not rinse.

instructions.name: Emulsify each bowl
instructions.text: Whisk 3/4 cup hot broth gradually into the sauce in each bowl, starting with a small splash so the sesame paste loosens smoothly. Divide the hot noodles among the bowls and stir once from the bottom to coat them.

instructions.name: Add the photographed finish
instructions.text: Spoon the pork mixture over the noodles. Finish each bowl with scallions, peanuts, sesame seeds and cilantro, matching the visible red broth and green garnish in the photograph. Serve immediately with extra chile oil and ground Sichuan pepper at the table.

why_it_works: Toasting whole Sichuan peppercorns briefly before grinding wakes up their citrusy aroma without letting the delicate spice scorch.
Browning the pork before adding garlic, ginger and doubanjiang prevents the aromatics from burning while the meat develops savory caramelized edges.
Whisking hot broth into the sesame paste a little at a time creates a smooth emulsion instead of oily clumps, giving the soup body without dairy.
Building the broth in individual bowls lets each diner adjust chile oil while keeping the shared pork topping flavorful but manageable.
swaps: Use ground turkey instead of pork; cook it to 165°F and add 1 extra teaspoon neutral oil because turkey is leaner.
For a meatless bowl, brown 12 ounces finely chopped shiitake and cremini mushrooms until their moisture evaporates, then continue with the aromatics and use vegetable broth.
Use well-stirred tahini if Chinese sesame paste is unavailable. Tahini is made from untoasted or lightly toasted sesame, so the finished broth will taste milder.
If sui mi ya cai is unavailable, use finely chopped preserved mustard greens and begin with 2 tablespoons; taste before adding more because brands vary widely in saltiness.
storage: For the best texture, refrigerate the pork topping, broth, sesame sauce and cooked noodles in separate shallow containers within 2 hours. Use within 3 days. Reheat the broth and pork together to 165°F, loosen the sesame sauce with a spoonful of hot broth and warm the noodles briefly in boiling water before assembling. Freezing is not recommended because the sesame emulsion can separate and the noodles become soft.
notes: Chinese sesame paste is made from deeply toasted sesame seeds and tastes stronger than tahini; stir the jar thoroughly before measuring because the oil separates.
Doubanjiang and preserved mustard greens are salty. Use low-sodium broth and soy sauce, cook the noodles in unsalted water and taste the assembled broth before adding any extra salt.
The calorie and cost estimates include the full pork topping, sauce and garnishes. Specialty pantry prices vary, but each jar supplies several future batches.

faqs.q: Can I make dan dan noodles mild?
faqs.a: Yes. Use 2 teaspoons doubanjiang in the pork and omit chile oil from the shared sesame base. Put chile oil and ground Sichuan pepper on the table so diners can increase both heat and numbing spice in their own bowls.

faqs.q: What is sui mi ya cai, and is it essential?
faqs.a: Sui mi ya cai is a finely chopped Sichuan preserved mustard green that adds concentrated savory, fermented flavor. It is traditional and useful here, but another preserved mustard green works; start with less, since salt levels differ by brand.

faqs.q: Why did my sesame broth look split or grainy?
faqs.a: The hot broth was probably added too quickly or the sesame paste was not fully stirred. Whisk in the first 2 tablespoons of broth until completely smooth, then add the remainder in a thin stream. The noodles and toppings can go in once the base is glossy.
